# Welcome

This tutorial walks through a complete **bulk RNA-seq** analysis on a real pediatric cancer dataset, **Wilms tumor** (the most common kidney cancer of childhood), with **limma**, one of the most widely used and best-documented tools for differential expression.

| Module | Question |
|--------|----------|
| **1 — Data and quality control** (this one) | What is in the expression matrix, and do the samples look the way we expect? |
| **2 — Differential expression with limma** | Which genes change between tumor and normal kidney, and between the two tumor histologies? |
| **3 — Gene set analysis** | Which biological programs do those changes point to? |

# Part 1 — The Dataset

The data come from **TARGET-WT**, the Wilms tumor project of the NCI's **TARGET** program (the pediatric counterpart of the adult-focused TCGA), downloaded from the **GDC Data Portal**. Tumors come from children enrolled in the Children's Oncology Group NWTS-5 trial.

All files are in `data/`, built by `data-prep/build_target_wt_data.R`:

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv` | 19,938 protein-coding genes × **124 tumors**, in TPM |
| `TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv` | the same genes × **6 normal kidney** samples ("Solid Tissue Normal"): all that exist for this project |
| `sample_metadata.csv` | one row per tumor: **histology** (Favorable / Unfavorable), age, sex, vital status |
| `TARGET_WT_control_clinical_raw.csv` | one row per normal sample, with the patient it comes from |

<div class="alert-info">
**Two histologies, two prognoses.** Wilms tumors are classified as **Favorable** histology (the large majority, with excellent survival) or **Unfavorable**, i.e. *anaplastic* (large, abnormal nuclei and chaotic mitoses). Anaplasia is the strongest adverse histological factor in Wilms tumor and drives more intensive treatment.
</div>

```{r load-data, echo=TRUE}
tumor_tpm   <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
control_tpm <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tumor_metadata   <- read_csv("data/sample_metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
control_metadata <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_clinical_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## TPM: What the Numbers Mean

Each value is a **TPM** (*transcripts per million*). For gene $i$ with $X_i$ reads and effective length $\ell_i$ (kb):

$$
\text{TPM}_i = \frac{X_i / \ell_i}{\sum_j X_j / \ell_j} \times 10^6
$$

1. **Divide by gene length**: a long gene collects more reads than a short one at the same expression level.
2. **Divide by the sample's total and multiply by one million**: removes the difference in sequencing depth between samples.

TPM values are already **normalized** and comparable across samples and genes; summed over all genes, every sample totals exactly one million.

<div class="alert-info">
**TPM and the choice of method.** Count-based methods (DESeq2, edgeR, limma-*voom*) model the number of **reads**, and their statistics rely on the noise of counting. TPM no longer carries that information: the read counts have been divided by gene length and library size. For TPM, the appropriate approach is to work on **log2(TPM + 1)** with a method designed for continuous, approximately normal data. That is exactly what **limma** was built for (originally for microarrays), and Module 2 uses its **limma-trend** variant.
</div>

# Part 2 — Building One Matrix and One Sample Sheet

Tumors and normals arrive as two files. We combine them into **one matrix** (genes × samples) and **one sample sheet** in the same order.

```{r combine, echo=TRUE}
# The two matrices must contain the same genes in the same order before being joined.
stopifnot(identical(tumor_tpm$gene_name, control_tpm$gene_name))

tpm <- as.matrix(bind_cols(tumor_tpm[, -1], control_tpm[, -1]))
rownames(tpm) <- tumor_tpm$gene_name

samples <- bind_rows(
  tumor_metadata %>% transmute(sample_id = case_submitter_id, patient = case_submitter_id,
                               group = histologic_subtype, sex = sex_at_birth, age_years),
  control_metadata %>% transmute(sample_id = sample_submitter_id, patient = case_submitter_id,
                                 group = "Control")
) %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("Control", "Favorable", "Unfavorable")))

# The sample sheet must follow the matrix columns exactly: limma matches them by position.
samples <- samples[match(colnames(tpm), samples$sample_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(samples$sample_id, colnames(tpm)))
```

```{r table-groups}
kable(count(samples, group, name = "samples"), caption = "Samples per group.")
```

```{r table-patients}
paired <- samples %>% group_by(patient) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>% arrange(patient, group) %>% ungroup()
kable(paired %>% select(patient, sample_id, group),
      caption = "Patients contributing two samples: each normal kidney comes from a child whose tumor is also in the dataset.")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**The design in one sentence.** 124 tumors (82 Favorable, 42 Unfavorable) and only **6 normal kidneys**, all from Favorable-histology patients who also contribute their tumor. The small control group limits every tumor-vs-normal comparison; the 6 tumor–normal **pairs** are not independent observations, and Module 2 shows how limma accounts for that.
</div>

# Part 3 — Sanity Checks

## TPM Totals

Our matrix keeps only **protein-coding** genes, so each sample sums to *somewhat less* than one million: the missing share is the sample's non-coding RNA. The totals should be similar across samples; a sample far off the rest has an unusual RNA composition.

```{r tpm-totals, echo=TRUE}
tpm_totals <- tibble(sample_id = colnames(tpm), total_tpm = colSums(tpm)) %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id")
```

```{r plot-tpm-totals, fig.height=4.5}
p_totals <- tpm_totals %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = total_tpm / 1e3, color = group, text = sample_id)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total protein-coding TPM (thousands)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(p_totals, tooltip = c("text", "y"))
```

## Filtering Low-Expressed Genes

Genes that are essentially not expressed carry no information but still count as tests, making the multiple-testing correction harsher for every other gene. We keep a gene if it has **TPM ≥ 1 in at least 6 samples**, the size of the smallest group, so a gene expressed only in normal kidney is still kept.

```{r filter, echo=TRUE}
min_samples <- min(table(samples$group))
keep <- rowSums(tpm >= 1) >= min_samples

# log2(TPM + 1): the scale used from here on. The +1 avoids log(0).
log_expr <- log2(tpm[keep, ] + 1)
```

```{r table-filter}
kable(tibble(step = c("Genes before", paste0("Genes kept (TPM >= 1 in >= ", min_samples, " samples)"), "Genes removed"),
             genes = c(length(keep), sum(keep), sum(!keep))),
      caption = "Effect of the expression filter.")
```

## Why the log Scale?

TPM values span six orders of magnitude, and their variance grows with their mean: a few very highly expressed genes would dominate any analysis on the raw scale. The log transform makes fold changes symmetric (doubling = +1, halving = −1) and the distribution much closer to the normal shape that linear models assume.

```{r plot-densities, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
bind_rows(
  tibble(value = as.vector(tpm[keep, ]), scale = "TPM"),
  tibble(value = as.vector(log_expr), scale = "log2(TPM + 1)")
) %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("TPM", "log2(TPM + 1)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 80, fill = "#2980b9") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gene × sample values") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

```{r plot-boxplots, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
as_tibble(log_expr, rownames = "gene") %>%
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "log_expr") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  mutate(sample_id = factor(sample_id, levels = samples$sample_id[order(samples$group)])) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_id, y = log_expr, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = "Samples", y = "log2(TPM + 1)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What to look for.** One box per sample, with medians at roughly the same height: the normalization worked and no sample is grossly different. A sample whose box sits clearly lower or higher than all others would be the first to investigate.
</div>

# Part 4 — Principal Component Analysis

PCA summarizes thousands of genes into a few axes of variation; each sample becomes a point, and similar samples land close together. We use the **1,000 most variable genes**, centered but not scaled (all genes are already on the same log2 scale).

```{r pca, echo=TRUE}
top_variable <- names(sort(apply(log_expr, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1000]
pca <- prcomp(t(log_expr[top_variable, ]), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)

percent_var <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1)
pca_scores  <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:4], rownames = "sample_id") %>% left_join(samples, by = "sample_id")
```

```{r plot-pca}
p_pca <- pca_scores %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = group, text = paste(sample_id, group, sep = " · "))) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", percent_var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", percent_var[2], "%)"), color = NULL,
       title = "PCA, 1,000 most variable genes") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_pca, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r plot-scree, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5}
tibble(PC = factor(paste0("PC", 1:10), levels = paste0("PC", 1:10)), variance = percent_var[1:10]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = variance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8e44ad") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Variance explained (%)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**How to read it.** The 6 normal kidneys separate clearly from the tumors: tumor vs normal is the strongest signal in the data. Favorable and Unfavorable tumors, instead, **overlap**: histology is *not* the main source of variation among tumors, which already tells us that their differences will be subtler. Tumors also spread widely: Wilms tumors mix blastemal, epithelial and stromal components in different proportions, and that composition, more than histology, drives much of the variation.
</div>

# Part 5 — Sample-Sample Correlation

For every pair of samples, the **Pearson correlation** of their log expression across all kept genes: 1 = identical profiles. The heatmap is clustered, so similar samples appear next to each other.

```{r correlation, echo=TRUE}
sample_cor <- cor(log_expr, method = "pearson")
```

```{r plot-correlation, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}
annotation <- data.frame(Group = samples$group, row.names = samples$sample_id)
heatmap_cor <- sample_cor
diag(heatmap_cor) <- NA

pheatmap(
  heatmap_cor,
  color = viridisLite::viridis(100), na_col = "white",
  clustering_distance_rows = as.dist(1 - sample_cor), clustering_distance_cols = as.dist(1 - sample_cor),
  clustering_method = "average",
  annotation_col = annotation, annotation_row = annotation,
  annotation_colors = list(Group = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")),
  annotation_names_row = FALSE, show_rownames = FALSE, show_colnames = FALSE,
  treeheight_row = 0, border_color = NA,
  main = "Sample-sample Pearson correlation (log2 TPM), clustered"
)
```

To spot single outliers, summarize each sample by its **median correlation with all the others**:

```{r median-correlation, echo=TRUE}
median_cor <- tibble(sample_id = colnames(heatmap_cor),
                     median_correlation = apply(heatmap_cor, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id")
```

```{r plot-median-correlation, fig.height=4.5}
p_med <- median_cor %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = median_correlation, color = group, text = sample_id)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median correlation with all other samples") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(p_med, tooltip = c("text", "y"))
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Flag, don't silently remove.** Normal kidneys correlate less with the rest simply because the rest are tumors. Among tumors, a sample far below its group is worth checking (RNA quality, tumor purity, a labeling error), but removing a sample is a decision that must be justified and reported: in a cohort this small, every sample matters.
</div>

# Summary

- One matrix (`r ncol(tpm)` samples) and one sample sheet, verified to match column by column.
- `r sum(keep)` genes kept after filtering, analyzed as **log2(TPM + 1)**.
- Tumor vs normal kidney is the dominant signal; Favorable and Unfavorable tumors overlap.
- Six patients contribute both a tumor and a normal sample.

Module 2 fits the limma model.
